summary: This document lists requirements for Ethernet VPN, driven by new uses such as data center interconnect and needs the current VPLS solution does not readily address, like all-active multihoming.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7209 describes what a better private Ethernet service would need to do. The service in use today, VPLS, can only have one provider router active at a time for a given customer, cannot make use of the label paths that would cut the number of multicast entries in the core, and still needs work on the network side of every connection. The RFC writes down the requirements a replacement would have to meet.

subtitle: What a better Ethernet VPN service would have to do that today's VPLS cannot.

tldr.problem: Virtual Private LAN Service is widely deployed, but it can only offer one active provider router per customer connection, it cannot use the multicast label paths that would cut core state, and it still needs configuration on both sides of a connection.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the requirements for Ethernet VPN: all-active multihoming with per-flow load balancing, faster convergence, less flooding, new service interface types for data centre interconnect, and tighter control of where a MAC address may appear.
tldr.outcome: The document is a requirements list, not a protocol. It carries the numbering from R1a through R14 and leaves the mechanism for each to the specifications that follow.

today: RFC 7209 is an Informational RFC published in May 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a requirements document: it defines no protocol, and the mechanism that satisfies each requirement is left to the specifications that follow it.

sections.title: What VPLS Cannot Do
sections.content:
Virtual Private LAN Service is a proven and widely deployed technology, but the existing solution has limitations around redundancy, multicast optimisation and provisioning simplicity. New applications also drive requirements for other Layer 2 VPN services, such as Ethernet Tree and Virtual Private Wire Service.

The RFC takes the gaps one at a time. On multihoming, current VPLS can only support the single-active redundancy mode, and the flexible multihoming with all-active mode cannot be supported at all. On multicast optimisation, an earlier document describes how multicast label switched paths can be used with VPLS, but that solution is limited to point-to-multipoint paths, because there is no defined way to use multipoint-to-multipoint paths with VPLS. On provisioning, current VPLS does offer single-sided provisioning through BGP-based service auto-discovery, but the operator still has to configure a number of network-side parameters on top of the access-side Ethernet configuration.

Applications also drive new service interface types. Data centre interconnect needs an interface that is a hybrid of VLAN bundling and VLAN-based service interfaces, which the RFC calls VLAN-aware bundling. Virtualization is increasing the number of MAC addresses the network has to handle, which gives rise to the requirement that the network reconverge after a failure in a time that does not depend on how many addresses the provider edge has learned. There are requirements to minimise the flooding of multi-destination frames and to keep that flooding inside the site where it started. And there are requirements for flexible VPN topologies and policies beyond what VPLS and hierarchical VPLS cover. The focus of the document is on defining the requirements for Ethernet VPN, which addresses these issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The service most providers sell has three known weaknesses: it is stingy with redundancy, it wastes core state on multicast, and it is not as automatic as it could be. Each weakness becomes a numbered requirement.

sections.title: Two Ways to Connect One Customer
sections.content:
The requirements turn on one distinction. In the single-active redundancy mode, a device or network is multihomed to a group of two or more provider edge routers, and only one of them forwards traffic to and from that device or network for a given VLAN. This is the mode that VPLS supports today.

In the all-active redundancy mode, the same arrangement applies, but every provider edge router in the group can forward traffic to and from the multihomed device for a given VLAN. The traffic is split between them, flow by flow, so that the links to the customer are all used and a failure of one of them does not stop the service.

The rest of the vocabulary is the ordinary Layer 2 VPN vocabulary: the customer edge device, the provider edge router it connects to, an autonomous system, a label switched path, a MAC address, multipoint-to-multipoint, and VPLS itself. An Ethernet Tree is the topology where one or more sites in the VPN are roots and the rest are leaves, with roots able to talk to other roots and to leaves, and leaves able to talk only to roots.
sections.plainLanguage: Single-active means one router in the group does the work. All-active means they all do, sharing the load and covering for each other when one fails.

sections.title: The Redundancy Requirements
sections.content:
The common way to multihome a customer device is with multi-chassis Ethernet link aggregation groups, where the load is spread across the links to the provider edge routers. The standard for link aggregation does not define a load-balancing algorithm, so implementations differ. All the RFC asks is that the algorithm keep each flow's frames in order. Typically the choice is made by hashing on some combination of the source and destination MAC addresses and VLAN at layer 2, the source and destination IP addresses at layer 3, and the source and destination port at layer 4. The first requirement is that a solution must support this flexible flow-based load balancing from the customer, and must also balance traffic destined to the customer across its links even when the customer is connected to more than one provider edge router.

Multipathing is the other half of the same idea: the solution must exercise all the label switched paths and all the equal-cost paths between a remote provider edge router and the members of the redundancy group. In the worked example, one customer device is multihomed to two provider edge routers and another to two more, with three equal-cost paths between any of them, and traffic can then travel over twelve different paths through the core.

The provider edge routers may sit in the same place or in different central offices, and a geographic spread is what gives business continuity during a power cut or a natural disaster. The solution must therefore support all-active multihoming without needing a dedicated link between the routers in the group, must support different interior gateway protocol costs to each of them, and must support multihoming across different interior gateway protocol domains within one autonomous system, and preferably across autonomous systems.

Traffic should also take the shortest sensible path: it should not be forwarded between provider edge routers in the same group unless the destination customer device is attached to one of them, which matters most when the routers are in different places, because forwarding between them adds latency and wastes switching capacity. The grouping itself should be flexible, so that a provider edge router can sit in several redundancy groups at once, for example a group of the first and second routers, a group of the first and third, and a group of the second and third. Finally, an entire Ethernet network may be multihomed rather than a single device, in which case the network usually runs a spanning tree or ring protection protocol, and those require each VLAN to be active on only one of the multihomed links. The solution must support the single-active mode with all VLANs on one router and with disjoint sets of VLANs on different routers, and may support the all-active mode for a network using MAC-based load balancing.
sections.plainLanguage: The redundancy requirements are about using every link the customer has, spreading the traffic by flow rather than by packet, and not sending traffic on a detour through a router that is next door when it does not have to.

sections.title: Multicast and Provisioning
sections.content:
Some environments would benefit from multipoint-to-multipoint label switched paths, because they would reduce the number of multicast states in the core routers. The earlier document on multicast in VPLS rules this out, because VPLS requires an egress provider edge router to learn MAC addresses when it receives unknown unicast packets over a path, and multipoint-to-multipoint paths have no inherent way to identify the sender. The way out is to lift that requirement, so the first requirement is that a solution must provide a way of receiving packets over a multipoint-to-multipoint path without MAC learning, and the second is that it should provide procedures for using those paths to deliver multicast, broadcast and unknown unicast traffic.

Provisioning has its own set of requirements. The solution must support auto-discovery of the provider edge routers belonging to a VPN over the core, in the same way as VPLS does, and should support auto-discovery of the routers in a given redundancy group. It should work out the site identifier of a multihomed device on its own and generate the group identifier from it, and should elect a designated forwarder among the routers in the group automatically and divide the service instances between them.

Where VLAN identifiers are global across the network, which limits the deployment to a maximum of 4K services, the routers should derive the MPLS-specific attributes such as the VPN identifier and the BGP route target from the VLAN identifier. The operator then configures only the VLAN on the access circuit and everything else follows. Implementations should also fall back on default values for any parameter that is not configured.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea here is that the operator should not have to tell the network twice. If the customer side says which VLAN, the network should work out the rest of the service by itself.

sections.title: The Service Interfaces
sections.content:
Three service types are already defined. In port mode, all the traffic on the port maps to a single bridge domain and a single Layer 2 VPN service instance, and customer VLAN transparency is guaranteed end to end. In VLAN mode, each VLAN on the port maps to its own bridge domain and service instance, which allows services to be multiplexed over the port and supports optional VLAN translation. In VLAN bundling, a group of VLANs on the port is mapped together to a single bridge domain and service instance, and customer MAC addresses must be unique across all the VLANs mapped to that instance. A single bridge domain is assigned per service instance on the provider edge router, whatever the number of VLANs arriving. A solution must support all three.

Data centre interconnect adds two more. Both bundle customer VLANs into a single Layer 2 VPN service instance and both keep the customer VLANs separated from each other in the data plane, by creating a dedicated bridge domain for each one. The difference is translation: the version with translation supports customer VLAN identifier translation, for the case where different identifiers are used on different interfaces for the same customer VLAN. The version without translation guarantees customer VLAN transparency end to end, and in the special case of all-to-one bundling the customer VLANs are not configured on the provider edge router at all, because the interface is configured just like a port-based service. Unlike the original three types, these new services need several bridge domains per service instance rather than one. The RFC says a solution may support VLAN-aware bundling.
sections.plainLanguage: There are now ways to offer the customer's VLANs to the network: one port, one VLAN, a bundle of VLANs, or a bundle where the network still keeps each VLAN apart. The last of these is what data centre interconnect asks for.

sections.title: Convergence, Flooding, Topology and Security
sections.content:
Convergence has to be quick and predictable. A solution must recover from a failure of the link between the customer and the provider edge router, and from the failure of a provider edge router, for both a multihomed device and a multihomed network. The recovery time must not depend on how many MAC addresses the provider edge router has learned, which matters more and more as virtualization multiplies the number of addresses, and should not depend on the number of service instances either.

Flooding should be under control. The operator should be able to choose per service instance whether unknown unicast frames are dropped or flooded. For data centre interconnect, the solution should keep broadcast frames inside the site that sent them, with the periodic address resolution traffic that every host sends being of particular interest. It should also stop unnecessary flooding of unicast traffic when the topology changes, especially at a multihomed site where the routers already know the backup paths for a given address.

Topology and policy are the last requirements before security. A solution must support VPN topologies that are not constrained by the mechanism used to implement them, with Ethernet Tree given as the example, where the solution must support it. It may apply policies per MAC address, so that only some member routers of the VPN learn a given address or send traffic for it. It must support both the option-C and the option-B inter-AS models.

On security, any protocol extensions must carry a proper security analysis, in addition to the security requirements of the documents that cover MAC learning in the data plane and in the control plane. Two requirements follow. A solution must be able to detect and handle the same MAC address appearing behind two different Ethernet segments, whether that happens by accident or on purpose. And it must be able to pin a MAC address to one Ethernet segment, which the RFC calls a sticky MAC, so that traffic for that address coming from any other segment is discarded and the address is not allowed to move.
sections.plainLanguage: Two themes run through the last requirements. Recovery should not get slower as the network learns more addresses, and the network should be able to notice when the same address turns up in two places at once, which is either a mistake or an attack.

left.title: Single-active
left.desc: Only one provider edge router in the group forwards traffic for a given VLAN. This is what VPLS offers today.

right.title: All-active
right.desc: Every provider edge router in the group forwards traffic, sharing it flow by flow so that a failure of one link does not stop the service.

viz.caption: THE REDUNDANCY REQUIREMENTS, R1 TO R6

items.title: Flexible load balancing
items.text: Spread the customer's traffic over its links by flow, using MAC, IP or port fields.

items.title: Multipathing
items.text: Use all the label switched paths and all the equal-cost paths to the group.

items.title: Geographic spread
items.text: Work with the routers in different places, without a dedicated link between them.

items.title: Optimal forwarding
items.text: Do not forward between routers in the group unless the destination is attached to one of them.

items.title: Flexible grouping
items.text: Let one router belong to several redundancy groups at once.

items.title: Multihomed networks
items.text: Support a whole Ethernet network being multihomed, not just one device.
